b.bio: The Puritan Thomas Watson was educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and from 1646 preached at St Stephen's, Walbrook, London. A Presbyterian with royalist sympathies, he was imprisoned in 1651 for his part in Christopher Love's plot to restore Charles II, released and formally reinstated vicar on 30 June 1652, and ejected for nonconformity at the Restoration. He kept preaching privately, opened a room for worship after the Great Fire of 1666, and after the Declaration of Indulgence of 1672 held a licence at Crosby House, where Stephen Charnock worked alongside him. The library also holds works by an earlier Thomas Watson — a mid-Tudor Catholic priest who preached before Queen Mary and published on the seven sacraments — and an Italian-madrigal translator of 1590; these are different men.
b.s: His works here are practical divinity: expositions of the beatitudes, the Shorter Catechism, repentance, contentment, and the godly character, arguing against Papists, Arminians, and Antinomians.

b.bio: Thomas Gale was born at Scruton, Yorkshire, educated at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow. He held the Regius Professorship of Greek at Cambridge from 1666 until he resigned it in 1672, then served as high master of St Paul's School, prebendary of St Paul's (1676), and from September 1697 Dean of York. He died at York on 7 April 1702. He was a classical scholar and antiquary who edited Greek and Latin authors and published collections of sources for early English history. The two pages this library holds under his name are editorial front matter in a Patrologia Latina volume, not a theological work of his own.
b.s: The item here is his editor's preface to a Latin patristic text, so he matters to readers as the scholar who prepared and introduced that edition rather than as a theologian.

b.bio: Thomas Hill was an English Puritan divine, born at Knighton-on-Teme, Worcestershire (one source gives Kington, Herefordshire), on the Herefordshire–Worcestershire border. Educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge (admitted pensioner 1618; BA 1622/23, MA 1626, BD 1633, and reportedly DD 1646), he served as Rector of Titchmarsh, Northamptonshire during the 1630s before returning to Emmanuel as Fellow and Master (c. 1644–45), then Master of Trinity College from 1645 until his death in December 1653; he was elected Vice-Chancellor of the university in 1646. He sat in the Westminster Assembly (sources give 1641 or 1643 for his appointment) and preached repeatedly before Parliament between 1642 and 1648.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly his published parliamentary fast sermons of the 1640s — on truth, church unity, separation, and sanctification — together with a compiled book of natural and artificial conclusions, showing a preacher who argued against Papists, Arminians, Saltmarsh, and Socinians while defending Christ's headship over the church.

b.bio: Thomas Cooper was born in Oxford, son of a poor tailor, and educated as a chorister at Magdalen College, where he became probationer, fellow, and master of the school. Under Mary he took a degree in physic and practised medicine in Oxford. Ordained about 1559, he rose under Elizabeth: Dean of Christ Church (1567), Dean of Gloucester (1569), Bishop of Lincoln (1571), and Bishop of Winchester from 1584 until his death on 29 April 1594. His Latin-English Thesaurus, known as Cooper's Dictionary, pleased Elizabeth I. The works here range from that lexicographical folio to sermons, an exposition of Old Testament chapters, and polemics against Martin Marprelate and the Papists.
b.s: He matters both as a bishop-theologian defending the Elizabethan settlement against Puritan and Roman critics and as author of the era's standard English-Latin dictionary; the library holds his great Thesaurus alongside his anti-Marprelate and anti-Papist polemics.

b.bio: This is not the Cambridge preacher Thomas Adams (1583–1652) described in the biographical sources; those dates and offices belong to a homonym. The works held here identify a different man: a City of London figure who in 1647 joined John Langham and James Bunce in petitioning against the army's interference with Parliament. The three were imprisoned loyalists whose cause the pamphlets defend as vindicated by providence.
b.s: His two works here are 1647 polemics on behalf of imprisoned London loyalists, arguing that the army's forced obedience subverted Parliament and fundamental laws and that divine judgment would charge civil ruin on its disobedience.

b.bio: The Thomas Carter of this library is not the Victorian tractarian Thomas Thellusson Carter described in The surviving records; those pages concern a different man of the same name and are disregarded here. The record's works decide who this is: a preacher and moral writer active in the late 1620s and early 1640s. In 1627 he published a large treatise on household duties, arguing from Scripture on marriage, parental authority, servants' patience under bad masters, and gratitude as both a natural and a commanded duty. In 1643 he preached at St Margaret's Westminster a sermon on prayer for Israel's safety.
b.s: His Christian common-wealth is a substantial Stuart domestic-morality treatise, treating anthropology, moral theology, the law, sin, prayer, providence, and the civil magistrate through household relations; the 1643 sermon documents Westminster preaching in the year it was printed.

b.bio: Thomas Cartwright (c. 1535–1603) was an English Puritan theologian and controversialist. He studied at St John's College, Cambridge, became a fellow of St John's and then Trinity College, and was appointed Lady Margaret's Professor of Divinity in 1569. His 1570 lectures made a public case for Presbyterian church government, and John Whitgift, as vice-chancellor, deprived him of the professorship in December 1570 and of his fellowship the next year. After publishing A Second Admonition to the Parliament in 1572 he left England. He spent his career in controversy with Whitgift over church polity and with Roman Catholic writers.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly his polemics against Whitgift on church government — asserting that Christ alone is head of the church and that word and sacrament ministry are inseparably joined — alongside later expository and devotional writings.

b.bio: The name means 'the king's reader' and is a title, not a personal name; no source gives dates or biography beyond Migne's dating of the letter to the fifth century (Saeculo V). The single epistle preserved in PL 72 is addressed by this palace official to bishops summoned to judge a dispute over property. He tells them he could have heard the case with his palace nobles (proceribus palatii mei), but because it concerns God and the clergy they should decide according to what they read in the Gospel and Paul's letter to the Corinthians, citing Aspar; he warns them not to fear his person, since they will render account before God, and asks that they leave senate, clergy, and people at peace.
b.s: A rare fifth-century imperial/palace voice instructing bishops to judge by the gospel rather than royal command, on church property and synodal authority.

b.t: 19th-century Anglican archivist (editor, not a Latin Father)
b.bio: Thomas Duffus Hardy, born at Port Royal, Jamaica, on 22 May 1804, entered government service as a junior clerk in the Tower of London Record Office in 1819 and was trained as an archivist by Henry Petrie. He edited numerous medieval records for the Record Commission, including the Close Rolls and Patent Rolls of King John, compiled the Monumenta Historica (1848), served as Deputy Keeper of the Public Record Office from 1861 until his death on 15 June 1878, and was knighted in 1873. He was an archivist and antiquary, not a patristic or medieval theologian; the 'Latin Fathers' shelfmark reflects Migne's Patrologia Latina printing, under which his editorial matter appears.
b.s: The library holds only his five-page Preface printed in PL 179; readers should treat him as the modern editor of the volume's contents rather than as its author.

b.bio: Theodorus Petreius (Latinized form of Peeters) was born April 17, 1567, at Kempen in Overijssel. After taking a master of arts at Cologne he entered the Carthusian convent there in 1587 and later served as prior of Dülmen in the bishopric of Münster, attending the order's general chapter twice. He died at Cologne April 20, 1640. He compiled devotional and apologetic works for the defence of the Catholic faith — Confessio Gregoriana, a Bibliotheca Cartusiana, a Chronologia of popes and emperors, and a Catalogus haereticorum — and edited the Opera omnia of St. Bruno of Cologne (Cologne, 1640). The pieces held here are prefatory matter from that edition.
b.s: He edited the Opera omnia of St. Bruno (Cologne, 1640); the items here are his letter 'To Saint Bruno' and address 'To the reader', plus an index arguing that the manuscripts attribute the exegetical works to Carthusian Bruno rather than Bruno of Segni.

b.bio: Thierry Ruinart was born at Reims on June 10, 1657 and entered the Maurist Congregation of the Benedictines at the Abbey of Saint-Remy, Reims on October 2, 1674. In 1682 he joined Jean Mabillon at the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, becoming his collaborator and later his biographer. He is best known for the Acta primorum martyrum sincera et selecta (first ed. Paris, 1689), a critical collection of genuine martyr acts whose introduction refuted Dodwell's De paucitate martyrum. He died at the Abbey of Hautvillers near Reims on September 27, 1709.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus for the Patrologia Latina: a Life of Urban II, historical commentary, prolegomena to Ivo of Chartres, an admonition, a dedicatory letter, and annotations, in which he weighs sources like Orderic Vitalis and Baronius on questions such as Urban II's birthplace and family and the date of Ivo's consecration.

b.bio: This entry is a corporate author, not an individual: the Roman Senate and People of the twelfth-century commune. the surviving records describe unrelated writers named Prudentius, Paulinus, Cyprian, and Jerome; none concerns this author and none is used here. The library holds one two-page text under this name in PL 204, a record of concord between the pope and the Roman senate.
b.s: The work held here is the sworn Concord between pope and senate: it records restoration of the city and coinage to the senate, return of regalia except the pons Lucanus, Tusculum's goods passing to the Roman church, an annual senatorial oath of fidelity to the pope, and mutual observance sanctioned by God and senate — directed against the Tusculans.

b.bio: Tomás Tamayo de Vargas (1588 or 1589 – 1641) was a Spanish diplomat, writer, and literary critic. He is not a Latin Father: Migne printed his Apospasmaton De Rebus Emeritensibus in PL 80 only as an appendix of learned notes on ancient Mérida (Emerita). The fragment argues that Augustus founded Emerita with discharged veterans, that the city's name derives from settled veterans (praemium being money, emeritum land), that it held the highest honors of Roman Lusitania and enjoyed ius italicum, and it defends these points against earlier writers including Tariphius Abentaquirius, Didacus de Valera, Franciscus Tarapha, Vinetus, and Petrus Merula, citing Strabo, Isidore, Tacitus, Pliny, Prudentius, Ausonius, Dio, and Suidas.
b.s: The work here is a humanist antiquarian treatise on Roman Mérida, preserved in the Patrologia Latina as an appendix rather than a patristic text.

b.bio: The library's record identifies this author as Tarra monachus, a sixth-century monk whose single surviving work is an epistle addressed to the Visigothic king Reccared, printed in PL 80 and dated by its editors to the sixth century (Corpus Corporum gives fl. 600). In the letter he writes under compulsion of the king's command rather than ambition, complains that he had been driven from his homeland and oppressed 'by the pontiff of the temple' before God sheltered him, and attacks the Caulianense monks while defending fidelity to one wife until death and God's protection of the innocent sufferer. He cites John and Isaiah.
b.s: His one-page epistle is a polemic against the Caulianense monks, framed as an unwilling obedience to King Reccared.

b.bio: Teraldus is a French (Francicus) Latin writer whose floruit falls in the tenth century; no dates, offices, or biography are recorded beyond this. The only work transmitted under his name is the Epistola ad Guidonem, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 138, columns 185–188B. The letter takes the form of a question and response on how the saints worship God: whether by faith alone or by faith joined with works. It argues that faith alone can please God without works, then distinguishes the two through liturgical exegesis — the canticle figures faith and the psalm figures works, verses with antiphons signify the pair together, and Paul exemplifies faith joined with almsgiving.
b.s: His single surviving letter is a compact tenth-century treatment of faith and works in worship, argued from the structure of the divine office rather than from later scholastic categories.

b.bio: Thegan of Trier, also printed as Degan of Treves, was a Frankish prelate from a noble family of the middle Rhine-Moselle region, possibly educated at Lorsch. By 825 he was auxiliary bishop of Trier and probably provost of St. Cassius at Bonn, though the identification with Theganbert is not certain. He was a friend of Walafrid Strabo, who edited his Gesta Hludowici imperatoris and gave it the title Gesta et Laudes.
b.s: His Life of Louis (Gesta Hludowici imperatoris), written 836–837, is a principal source for the reign of Louis the Pious; it is a partisan defense of Louis that attacks Lothair and Ebo of Reims, and its theses on papal consecration of emperors and kings make it important for medieval political theology.

b.bio: Theobald of Bec, a Norman monk of the Abbey of Bec who became its abbot in 1137, was elected Archbishop of Canterbury on 28 December 1138 and consecrated on 8 January 1139. He served through the civil war of King Stephen's reign: he defied the king by attending Pope Eugene III's council at Reims in 1148 and, on papal orders, refused to crown Stephen's son Eustace in 1152, helping force the settlement that brought Henry of Anjou to the throne. He was named papal legate around 1150 and gathered scholars in his household, including his successor Thomas Becket.
b.s: The letters and testament held here document how an archbishop navigated church-state conflict under Stephen and helped secure the Angevin succession; Theobald's household also shaped the next generation of English clergy and jurists.

b.bio: Theobald of Étampes (Theobaldus Stampensis) was a secular clerk and schoolmaster, a canon's son from Étampes, probably educated at the Chartres Cathedral School. He studied and later taught at Caen in Normandy, then moved to Oxford between 1096 and 1102, where he taught theology for at least thirty years and claimed to have lectured to sixty or a hundred students — the first scholar known to have lectured there.
b.s: He is remembered as the earliest known Oxford lecturer and a forerunner of the university; the letters held here are polemical responses defending confession of heart over vocal confession when the voice is lacking, arguing that God judges by will not deed, and attacking Roscelin and other innovating teachers.

b.bio: Thierry of Chartres (Theodoricus Carnotensis) taught at Chartres and Paris in the mid-twelfth century and succeeded Gilbert of Poitiers as chancellor at Chartres around 1141. He was a Platonist who read Genesis through Plato's Timaeus, compiled the Heptateuchon for teaching the liberal arts, and counted John of Salisbury among his pupils. The single item this library holds under his name is not one of those works but a one-page privilege for Vendôme monastery printed in PL 157.
b.s: A leading figure of the school of Chartres whose theological writings applied Platonic natural philosophy to creation and the Trinity; the work held here, however, is only a short monastic charter, not a treatise.

b.bio: Theodoric (Dietrich) I of Metz was a Saxon nobleman, son of Count Everard and a cousin of Emperor Otto the Great and Bruno of Cologne. He became Bishop of Metz in 964, succeeding Adalbero I, founded the abbey of St Vincent at Metz, and assembled a large collection of relics for it. In 978 he crowned Charles, Duke of Lower Lorraine, as king at Laon. Sigebert of Gembloux and Alpert of Metz wrote biographies of him.
b.s: The works here are hagiographical: The Finding of the Saints argues that incorrupt, fragrant relics and miracles attest sanctity even without a written life, and that relic authenticity is confirmed by a bishop's oath on the Gospels — fitting testimony from a bishop who gathered relics for St Vincent's.

b.bio: A monk of the abbey of St. Eucharius at Trier. He composed an account of the discovery and translation of relics of St. Celsus, found in a sarcophagus during the rebuilding of the abbey church after Archbishop Egbert of Trier's reform of the abbey in 978. The DLL catalog dates his activity to the tenth century, but the works held here are polemics against Hildebrand that invoke Henry IV, which points to an eleventh-century (Investiture Controversy) context.
b.s: His surviving works here are local Trier hagiography and polemic from the Investiture Controversy era: a defense against opponents including Hildebrand and certain Trier clergy, and an account of the cult of St. Celsus, which may include one of the earliest recorded uses of fire ordeal to authenticate relics.

b.bio:
Theodgaud I of Belgic Gaul (d. 868) — Theodgaud (Theutgaud) was archbishop of Trier from 850, succeeding his uncle Hetto, and previously abbot of Mettlach. He claimed primacy for Trier over Rheims, drawing opposition from Hincmar of Rheims. In June 863 he and Gunther of Cologne presided over the synod of Metz that sanctioned Lothair II's repudiation of his wife Teutberga in favor of Waldrada. Summoned to Rome, he was condemned at the Lateran Synod of October 863 by Pope Nicholas I, who deposed him; he died in 868. The two epistles held here are joint letters of Theodgaud with Gunther of Cologne, Arduicus of Besançon, Rotlandus of Arles, and Tado of Milan, addressed to the bishops of King Louis's realm.

Gunther of Cologne (d. 873) — Gunther (Gunthar) belonged to a noble Frankish family and was consecrated Archbishop of Cologne on 22 April 850. He resisted ceding Bremen to Ansgar until Pope Nicholas I settled the matter around 860. As arch-chaplain to King Lothair II, he led the Aachen synods of 860 that compelled Queen Teutberga's confession and permitted the king to discard her. Gunther was excommunicated and deposed in 863. He died 8 July 873.

Ardu (unknown) — Two short epistles under this name stand in PL 121. They deal with canonical procedure: an accuser who fails to prove his charge incurs a penalty, accusations against a bishop must be judged at a synod, causes of absent disputants must not be rashly judged, the apostolic see may revise judgments reached through deception, an unjust depositor is condemned while coerced consenters are excused, a deposed cleric is not restored without his bishop's consent, a condemned priest is reconciled after the statutory delay, and a bishop may not seize another bishop's cleric. The chief opponents named are Hincmar of Reims and Rothad of Soissons, whose conflict over Rothad's deposition is usually dated to the 860s. This material does not fit Ardo Smaragdus, monk and abbot of Aniane (died March 843), who wrote the Vita of Benedict of Aniane; the attribution of these letters to him is doubtful, and the author behind them cannot be identified from the sources given.
b.s: The works held are the joint Carolingian epistles defending canonical procedure against Hincmar's excommunication of Rothad — asserting that accusations against bishops must be judged at synods, that failed accusers incur penalty, and that the apostolic see may revise its own deceived judgments.

b.bio: Theodoric III (Theuderic III), son of Clovis II and Balthild of the Merovingian dynasty, was appointed king in Neustria in 673 by Ebroin, mayor of the palace, was soon displaced by his brother Childeric II, was restored in 675, and after Dagobert II's death in 679 was also recognized as king in Austrasia. Sources describe him as a puppet ruler (roi fainéant) under mayors of the palace; his army under mayor Berchar was defeated by Pepin of Heristal at Tertry in 687. The work held here consists of royal precepts and judgments concerning churches and monasteries — grants of land, immunities from exaction, and jurisdiction — issued in the king's name.
b.s: His precepts are primary evidence for how Merovingian kingship exercised piety through legal protection of monasteries and episcopal rights, including disputes with figures such as Duke Adalric and Bishop Chramlin of Embrun.

w: Fragments of the metrical life of St. Ouen

b.bio: This Theodoric is not the twelfth-century philosopher Theodoric of Chartres described in three of The surviving records; those sources concern a different man with a similar name and are set aside. What can be said comes from the library record alone: this author composed a metrical life of St. Ouen (Audoenus), of which only fragments survive in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 150). The fragments recount the translation of the saint's relics, insisting that heaven forbids separating Ouen's head from his body and that divine power fixes where his church should stand.
b.s: His fragments are evidence for early medieval relic-translation piety: they assert that holy places confer healing and salvation and that monasteries were founded at miracle sites.

w: Letter to the people of Liège

b.bio: Abbot of the imperial abbey of Saint-Hubert at Andage in the Ardennes during the Investiture Conflict. The sources show him navigating between obedience to the bishop of Liège, papal protection, and appeal to Rome. He should not be confused with Thierry of Chartres, the twelfth-century Platonist schoolman, nor with the later Blessed Theodoric of Saint-Hubert (born 1067, abbot 1087) described in hagiographical sources.
b.s: His letter to the people of Liège survives in PL 157 as evidence of how an imperial-abbatial community under an Investiture-era abbot addressed the laity of its diocese.

b.bio: Theodoric, son of Thiudimer (Theodemir), was king of the Ostrogoths from 471 or 474/475. Sent as a boy as hostage to Constantinople, he received an East Roman education; Emperor Zeno later made him magister militum (483) and consul (484). At Zeno's direction he led his people into Italy in 488 against Odoacer, completing the conquest by 493 and ruling Italy until his death at Ravenna in August 526. He used only the title rex, though Italian aristocrats called him princeps and he exercised quasi-imperial powers. The works held here are his precepts — royal orders issued under his name, preserved in PL 72.
b.s: These four short precepts show an Arian barbarian king legislating on ecclesiastical discipline: councils must reconvene where first summoned, definitions made under discord are uncertain, bishops are the proper judges of doctrine, emperors must not judge ecclesiastical causes, prelates may not alienate church property by usufruct, and alienated church property must be reclaimed with its fruits according to the donor's intent.

w: Chapters presented to the Council of Hertford

b.bio: Born at Tarsus in Cilicia around 602, Theodore was a monk living in Rome when Pope Vitalian chose him for the see of Canterbury; he was consecrated on 26 March 668 and reached England in May 669. Bede credits him with visiting the whole island, filling vacant bishoprics, and regularizing an English Church still disordered after the Paschal controversy. He founded a school at Canterbury teaching biblical commentary, Roman law, and Greek.
b.s: The works held here are his disciplinary and penitential legislation — chapters and canons, including those presented to the Council of Hertford — which established ecclesiastical law and penitential practice for the English Church. The texts treat confession to God alone as sufficient when necessary, graded penitential fasts, and redemption of penance by psalms and alms.

b.bio: A Greek born in Jerusalem, son of a bishop named Theodore; he came to Rome among the clergy displaced by the Muslim conquests and was made cardinal by John IV. Elected pope in November 642 with the exarch of Ravenna's confirmation, he spent his pontificate opposing Monothelitism: he refused to recognize Patriarch Paul of Constantinople because Pyrrhus's deposition had not been canonical, pressed Constans II to withdraw the Ecthesis, received Pyrrhus's recantation in 645, and excommunicated him when he relapsed in 648.
b.s: The three letters here concern monastic exemption: they assert that the apostolic see grants privileges protecting monastic vows, that neighboring bishops have no power over exempt monasteries, that chrism and ministries come from prelates of the monastery's choosing, that the abbot is elected by his congregation and ordained within the monastery, and that correction belongs to the abbot and abbatial correction to the pope—grounded in Peter's power of binding and loosing—and they argue against Pyrrhus and against bishops claiming jurisdiction over monasteries, citing Chalcedon, the five holy councils, Columbanus, King Rotharis, and Queen Gundiberga.

b.bio: Theodosius I (c. 347–c. 346) — Flavius Theodosius, born at Cauca in Gallaecia (Spain) on 11 January 347 (older authorities give c. 346), son of the general Comes Theodosius. After service against the Sarmatians as Dux of Moesia and a period of retirement following his father's execution (376), Gratian named him Augustus for the East on 19 January 379 after Valens died at Adrianople. He ruled the East from 379 to 392 and was sole emperor from 392 until his death at Milan on 17 January 395, succeeded by Arcadius and Honorius. He established the Nicene Creed as the norm of orthodoxy and convened the Council of Constantinople (381).
b.s: The two volumes here hold his imperial legislation rather than theology: decrees on religion and true worship directed against Manichaeans, Arians, and all dissenters from the Nicene faith, alongside administrative laws on provincial accounts, negligent judges, judicial procedure, palatine office, Sunday observance, and legal holidays.

b.bio: Theoger, born around the middle of the eleventh century, was a canon at St. Cyriacus in Worms before entering the abbey of Hirsau under Abbot William, who made him prior of Reichenbach. In 1088 he became third abbot of St. Georgen in the Black Forest, which under him became a center of the so-called St. Georgen reform spreading through Alsace, southern Germany, and Austria. Elected bishop of Metz in 1117 and consecrated the following year, he never entered his see because of the Investiture Controversy and died on 29 April 1120, reportedly at Cluny. A Vita by a monk of Prüfening (attributed to Wolfger, though doubted) was written between 1138 and 1146, within about two decades of his death.
b.s: The library holds an eight-page music treatise printed under his name in PL 163: definitions and proofs on strings, tones, semitones, and intervals (diatessaron, diapente, diapason), citing Boethius and Guido against unnamed moderns.

b.bio: Theologi Duacenses ('theologians of Douai') is a collective printed signature for theologians of Douai who prepared an edition of the Ordinary Gloss on Scripture. The four-page address 'To the reader' held here defends Walafrid Strabo's authorship of the Ordinary Gloss while conceding it was enlarged by later hands, argues that manuscript collation restores the true gloss text, and insists that only the fathers belong in the gloss's chain of authorities. It polemicizes against Matthias Tornigius (Dornick), Paul of Burgos, Sixtus Senensis, and the Parisian printers and editors.
b.s: The work here is an editorial preface defending the patristic character and textual integrity of the Ordinary Gloss against rival editions and critics.

b.bio:
Theophilus (unknown) — The library holds under the name 'Theophilus' a six-page Life of St. Macarius from PL 73, treating prayer, fasting, the sign of the cross against demons, and the cherubim guarding paradise. No surviving record connects this text to any known Theophilus. The sources instead describe two other men: Theophilus of Antioch, second-century bishop of Antioch and apologist whose sole surviving work is Ad Autolycum, and Theophilus Presbyter (fl. c. 1070–1125), pseudonymous author of De diversis artibus on the mechanical arts. Neither wrote a life of Macarius, so neither source can establish authorship of the held work.

Sergius (unknown) — The library holds one short work under this name: a six-page Life of St. Macarius printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 73. the surviving records all concern Pope Sergius I of Rome (687–701), a different person, and therefore cannot be used to describe this author. Nothing beyond the library record is available, so the author's dates, origin, and office cannot be stated.

Hyginus (c. c. 138–142) — The name Hyginus attaches in early Christian literature to more than one figure. The best-documented is Pope Hyginus, bishop of Rome c. 138–142 (some authorities give c. 136–140 or c. 137–141; the chronology cannot be fixed exactly), a Greek by birth according to the Liber Pontificalis, whose pontificate saw Valentinus and Cerdo teaching gnostic doctrine at Rome. But that pope left no writings, and the work held here — a six-page Latin Life of St. Macarius recounting the monk's renunciation of the world, preservation through fasting and peril, angelic guardianship, cherubim guarding paradise, and the sign of the cross against demons — cannot be attributed to him on any source evidence. The author of this life remains unidentified; readers should not conflate him with the second-century bishop.
b.s: The single work held here is hagiography about Macarius of Egypt, not the apologetic or technical writing associated with either namesake in the sources; its authorship remains unestablished.

b.bio: Theudoin of Châlons (Theudoinus Catalaunensis) was a provost at Châlons-sur-Marne, documented on 25 March in a year given variously as 868 or 878. He is known from a single letter to Almannus, a monk of Hautvillers, describing how the removal of a mausoleum and earth revealed the tomb of Saint Memmius, first bishop of Châlons. The letter recounts the finding of the saint's body in a stone-lined grave and attributes the event to God's hidden providence.
b.s: His surviving epistle is a contemporary witness to the ninth-century translation and cult of Saint Memmius, patron of the diocese of Châlons.

w: Questions on the Books of Kings

b.bio:
Theutmirus (d. 840) — Theutmirus was a Catholic monk of the Carolingian period who died in 840. The Wikisource record lists a single work by him, the Quaestiones super libros Regum, questions on the books of Kings. Nothing further about his life, monastery, or office is given in the sources consulted.

Claudius of Turin (fl. 810–827) — Claudius of Turin was a bishop and exegete, probably born near Seo de Urgel in Spain and educated among the clerics of Felix of Urgel. He trained at the school of Leidradus at Lyons, then served as a priest at the court of Louis the Pious in Aquitaine and later at Aachen, where he taught. He became bishop of Turin in 817 or 818 and held the see until his death toward the end of 827. As bishop he attacked the cult of images and relics; Dungal and Jonas of Orléans wrote against him as a heretic on that score. His biblical commentaries are collectanea—catenae compiled from patristic sentences.
b.s: His surviving work here is a set of scriptural questions on the books of Kings, preserved in PL 104.

w: Prologue to the exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict

b.t: Latin (listed by Migne as 'Theuzo Eremita'; monastic order unconfirmed)
b.bio: Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 143) lists one work under the name Theuzo the Hermit: a prologue to an exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict, dated 1057. No source confirms any Florentine house for this author; the Florence Cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, and Marianus of Florence materials concern other subjects entirely. Per the library record, the prologue says the exposition is compiled from earlier fathers' labors and argues that unwillingness, not obscurity, keeps readers from the Rule.
b.s: His single surviving piece is a mid-eleventh-century witness to how Benedict's Rule was glossed from patristic authorities, citing Gregory above all.

b.bio: Thiepaldus (Thietpald) of Tegernsee is known only from a single Latin letter dated to 1003, addressed to Saint Adalbert as bishop of the Prussian church. He was a writer at the abbey of Tegernsee. He should not be confused with Thietpald, abbot of Saint Gall (died 1034), nor with Metellus of Tegernsee, the twelfth-century poet of the same house.
b.s: The library holds his one surviving work, a letter to Saint Adalbert on the Prussian mission, which cites Aristotle and Plato.

w: Letter to the archbishops and bishops

b.bio: The works held under this name in PL 155 belong to a late eleventh-century English churchman, not to the thirteenth-century Franciscan theologian Thomas of York described in surviving records; those sources concern a different person and cannot be used for this author. On the evidence of the library record alone, this Thomas appears as a correspondent of Lanfranc and an associate of Bishop William of Durham and King William.
b.s: His letters defend monastic exemption from episcopal exactions and compulsory synod attendance, and his epitaph of King William is a contemporary historical witness (per the library record).

w: History of the Monastery of Hasnon

b.bio: The library prints this name as Thomas of Hasnon; the sources give it as Tomellus Hasnoniensis, and the subject matter matches the work held here, so they are evidently the same author. He was secretary to Baldwin VI, count of Flanders and Hainaut, and wrote his History of the Monastery of Hasnon at the request of Abbot Roland (died c. 1085), covering the restoration of the abbey from 1070 onward. It was composed in part from the abbey's archives, and the work itself insists that history must rest on archival evidence, not invention. The work defends the restored Benedictine house against its former canons and against Winthericus's kinsmen, and justifies rule of a double monastery by both sexes.
b.s: His single surviving work is a primary source for the 11th-century restoration of Hasnon Abbey under the counts of Flanders.

b.bio: Trifolius was a sixth-century Christian theologian, a presbyter possibly of Rome. In 519/520 he wrote a letter from Rome to the Roman senator Faustus against the monk John the Scythian, reporting on the doctrine of the Scythian monks who had come from Constantinople teaching that 'one of the Trinity was crucified.' Trifolius argues that this Theopaschite formula is not found in the four ecumenical councils, was already condemned at Chalcedon (as against the Eutychians Carosus and Dorotheus), and proceeds from the font of Arius, comparing the Scythians' Trinitarian teaching with Arian and Apollinarian views. The letter played a part in the rejection of the Theopaschite doctrine.
b.s: His single surviving work is a contemporary anti-Theopaschite report on the Scythian monks' formula Unus ex Trinitate passus est. According to the library record, Trifolius distinguishes between 'one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh,' which he allows may admit an orthodox sense, and 'one of the Trinity was crucified,' which he treats as an Arian heresy; he frames the formula's Trinitarian teaching as Arian in origin and as already condemned by Chalcedon.

b.bio: Trojanus of Saintes (also Trojan, Troyen) was a sixth-century bishop of Saintes in western France, mentioned in semi-legendary terms by Gregory of Tours and commemorated as a Catholic saint with a feast on November 30. He is identified with the author of a surviving letter to Eumerius of Nantes, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 67. Catholic Online gives his death as 533 and adds hagiographical detail (a Jewish father and Arabic mother) that the other sources do not confirm.
b.s: His letter to Eumerius is one of the few surviving Gallic episcopal texts on baptismal discipline: it argues that doubtful baptism requires rebaptization without delay and that neglect of baptism endangers souls and blames pastors, citing Pope Leo I.

b.bio: Turcius Rufius Apronianus Asterius was a Roman aristocrat under Theodoric the Great, urban prefect before holding the consulship in 494 with Flavius Praesidius. His subscription correcting the fifth-century codex Mediceus of Vergil records his literary activity, and an elegiac poem commemorates the consular games he gave at great expense to his fortune. McClintock and Strong report that out of office he edited poems of Sedulius, including a Collection of the Old and New Testaments in elegiac verse sometimes printed under his own name and by some ascribed to him. He is distinct from Flavius Asturius, consul in 449.
b.s: The epigrams held here are editorial-critical pieces on Sedulius's biblical elegiac verse, arguing for Asterius's authorship or editorship against Barthius, Labbeus, Cellarius, Gallandius, Arntzen, and pagan readings.

b.bio: Turgot was born in Lincolnshire to a Saxon family of good standing. Held as a hostage after the Norman Conquest, he escaped to Norway, where he taught psalmody to King Olaf III. He returned to England around 1074, became a monk at Wearmouth via Jarrow, and in 1087 was made prior of Durham, serving nearly twenty years and helping lay the foundation stone of Durham Cathedral in 1093. A friend and spiritual adviser of St Margaret of Scotland, he wrote her vita between 1100 and 1107 at the request of Queen Matilda. In 1107 he was elected Bishop of St Andrews; consecration was delayed by disputes between York and St Andrews until 1 August 1109.
b.s: The work held here is his account of Bede's life and burial, defending the tradition that Bede's relics rest with Cuthbert at Durham against those who placed them in Rome.

b.bio: Turibius was an archdeacon of Tui before becoming Bishop of Astorga in Gallaecia. He held a local synod in 446 and led the Nicene opposition to Priscillianism in northwestern Hispania, for which Pope Leo the Great wrote him a supportive letter on the errors of the Priscillianists that still survives. He died at Astorga in 460 and was venerated as a saint; tradition holds his relics, with a relic of the cross he brought from Jerusalem, were moved to Liébana in the eighth century.
b.s: His surviving epistle is a witness to the anti-Priscillianist campaign in fifth-century Gallaecia and to the discipline Turibius sought to enforce as bishop.

w: On the feast of Saint Othmar
Verses on the Nativity of the Lord
Verses on the Reception of the Prince

b.bio: Tutilo (Tuotilo) was a monk of the Benedictine abbey of Saint Gall, educated there under Iso of St. Gallen and Moengal and a close friend of Notker the Stammerer. Ekkehard IV, writing a century later, describes him as strong, ready of speech, a carver and painter, and a musician who taught the harp to noble pupils in a cell granted by the abbot. Sources give differing death dates — 915 in Wikipedia and Britannica, c. 913 in the CERL Thesaurus. The works held here are Latin poems on liturgical and occasional subjects.
b.s: He is credited with inventing tropes for liturgical chant, and the verses held here show his occasional and festal Latin poetry.

b.bio: Theophilus became Patriarch of Alexandria in 385 and held the see until his death on 15 October 412; his successor was his nephew Cyril. Jerome notes he did not appear as a public teacher before his election in 385. His patriarchate is tied to three events: the destruction of pagan temples in Egypt, including the temple of Serapis around 391 with imperial permission from Theodosius I; the Origenist controversy, in which he turned against the monks he had earlier defended; and the deposition and banishment of John Chrysostom, secured through intrigue at Constantinople. The library holds a single short item from PG 65: fragments chiefly concerned with the paschal computation and the observance of Sunday.
b.s: The work here preserves his paschal epistles and related fragments — including the claim that he compiled a 418-year paschal cycle — alongside material on Sunday as both first and eighth day, the restoration of lapsed clergy, and arguments against Origen.

w: Theodulus the Monk, or Thomas Magister

b.bio: Thomas Magister, a native of Thessalonica born around 1270–1280, was a Byzantine grammarian and confidential adviser to Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos, holding court office before taking monastic vows as Theodulus by 1328. He taught a circle of students including Philotheus Coccinus and Gregory Acindynus, compiled an Attic lexicon from Phrynichus, Ammonius, Herodian and Moeris, and wrote scholia on Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes. A manuscript inscription dated 1342–43 has traditionally been taken to describe him as blind in Thessalonica, though its trustworthiness has been questioned; Acindynus corresponded with him in 1347–48, which gives a terminus post quem for his death. The volume held here is his encomiastic oration on Gregory Nazianzen, defending praise of the saints as a duty against those who would keep silent.
b.s: The work held here is his panegyric on Gregory of Nazianzus, arguing that honoring the saints is obligatory speech rather than rashness, and citing Plato, Homer and the tragedians alongside Gregory himself.

b.bio: A Theophanes, Archbishop of Nicaea, whose single surviving work held here argues against the Palamites and against 'new Nestorians,' opponents that place him in or after the fourteenth-century Palamite controversy. No source gives his birth or death dates. A monograph by Ioannis D. Polemis treats 'Theophanes of Nicaea: His Life and Works,' but the surviving account does not confirm biographical details, so his identity rests on the library record itself. He should not be confused with Saint Theophanes the Confessor and Hymnographer, Bishop of Nicea (d. after 842), the iconoclast-era confessor described in other sources.
b.s: His single work held here is a dogmatic treatise treating sin, Christology, grace, last things, church, sacraments, anthropology, virtues/moral theology, sanctification, and Scripture, written against the Palamites, 'new Nestorians,' deniers of real divine attributes, Origen, Consalvus Ponce de Leon, and the devil.
